Kot.et: From Middle High German quāt, from Old High German quāt, from Proto-West Germanic *kwād.

Kotflügel.et: Probably because one of its functions at invention time was to keep feces (Kot) from the street away from the passengers of the first, quite open cars.

kotzen.et: From an earlier koptzen, from Middle High German koppezen, intensive form of koppen (“to spit”), likely of onomatopoeic origin.

Kotze.et: From Middle High German kotze, from Old High German chozzo, probably from Old French cotte (“overshirt”).

Koteletten.et: 19th century, from French côtelettes (“sideburns”, literally “cutlets”), humorously after the form, invoking the idea of two cutlets glued to the sides of the face. In French an exclusively informal and now apparently archaic use.

Köter.et: Borrowed from Low German Köter, from Middle Low German kȫter. Standard use since the 18th century. Further origin uncertain. Perhaps imitative of panting.

Kotau.et: Ultimately from Chinese 叩頭 /叩头 (kòutóu), possibly through English kowtow.

s: tenant; cotter (farmer who dwells and works on a parcel of a wealthier farmer’s land)
Kötter.et: Borrowed from Middle Low German [Term?]. Derived from the noun kotte, kōte (“hut, cottage”), whence German Kate (“hut”). Compare English cotter.
